concepts.name: Scarcity
concepts.description: Resources are limited while human wants are unlimited, forcing individuals, firms, governments and societies to make choices and incur trade‑offs.

concepts.name: Opportunity Cost
concepts.description: The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made; it reflects the forward‑looking cost of sacrificing one option for another.

concepts.name: Positive Economics
concepts.description: Economic statements that can be tested and verified with empirical evidence, describing how the economy actually works.

concepts.name: Normative Economics
concepts.description: Economic statements that involve value judgments about what ought to happen, reflecting policy goals and ethical considerations.

concepts.name: Production Possibility Frontier
concepts.description: A graphical model showing the maximum feasible combinations of two goods an economy can produce given its resources and technology; it illustrates scarcity and trade‑offs.

concepts.name: Economic Growth
concepts.description: An increase in an economy’s capacity to produce goods and services over time, shifting the PPF outward through better technology, resources, or institutions.

concepts.name: Demand
concepts.description: The quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to purchase at various prices during a given period, holding other factors constant.

concepts.name: Supply
concepts.description: The quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to sell at various prices during a given period, holding other factors constant.

concepts.name: Market Equilibrium
concepts.description: The price and quantity at which the amount consumers want to buy equals the amount producers want to sell; deviations create surplus or shortage pressures.

concepts.name: Demand Shift
concepts.description: A change in demand caused by a determinant other than the good’s own price (e.g., income, preferences, number of buyers), moving the entire demand curve.

concepts.name: Supply Shift
concepts.description: A change in supply caused by a determinant other than the good’s own price (e.g., input costs, technology, taxes), moving the entire supply curve.

concepts.name: Price Elasticity of Demand
concepts.description: A measure of how responsive quantity demanded is to a percentage change in price; classified as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic.

concepts.name: Total Revenue
concepts.description: The total amount received by sellers from sales (price multiplied by quantity sold); its movement depends on the price elasticity of demand.

concepts.name: Income Elasticity of Demand
concepts.description: A measure of how quantity demanded responds to changes in consumer income; positive values indicate normal goods, negative values inferior goods.

concepts.name: Cross‑Price Elasticity of Demand
concepts.description: A measure of how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good; positive values indicate substitutes, negative values complements.

concepts.name: Utility
concepts.description: A representation of the satisfaction or benefit a consumer derives from consuming goods and services; underlies consumer choice analysis.

concepts.name: Budget Constraint
concepts.description: The set of consumption bundles a consumer can afford given income and prices; changes in income or a price pivot the constraint.

concepts.name: Consumer Equilibrium
concepts.description: The point at which a consumer selects the affordable bundle that maximizes total utility, typically where an indifference curve is tangent to the budget line.

concepts.name: Indifference Curve
concepts.description: A curve showing all combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction; downward sloping, reflecting trade‑offs.

concepts.name: Marginal Rate of Substitution
concepts.description: The rate at which a consumer is willing to give up one good for another while remaining equally satisfied; equal to the slope of the indifference curve.

concepts.name: Substitution and Income Effects
concepts.description: The decomposition of a price change’s impact on consumption into a substitution effect (relative price change) and an income effect (purchasing‑power change).

concepts.name: Marginal Utility
concepts.description: The additional utility obtained from consuming one more unit of a good; the principle of diminishing marginal utility states this typically declines after a point.

concepts.name: Factors of Production
concepts.description: The resources used to produce goods and services: land (natural resources), labor (human effort), capital (machinery, buildings), and entrepreneurship (organizing and bearing risk).

concepts.name: Productivity
concepts.description: The amount of output generated per unit of input; it can rise through better technology, skills, management, or capital.

concepts.name: Short Run
concepts.description: A time period in which at least one input (typically capital) is fixed while others can be varied.

concepts.name: Long Run
concepts.description: A time period in which all inputs can be adjusted; firms can change plant size, technology, and all other factors.

concepts.name: Fixed Costs
concepts.description: Costs that do not vary with the level of output in the short run (e.g., rent, salaries).

concepts.name: Variable Costs
concepts.description: Costs that change directly with the level of output (e.g., raw materials, labor hours).

concepts.name: Total Cost
concepts.description: The sum of fixed and variable costs for a given level of production.

concepts.name: Average Total Cost
concepts.description: Total cost divided by the quantity of output; indicates per‑unit cost.

concepts.name: Marginal Cost
concepts.description: The additional cost incurred by producing one more unit of output; often U‑shaped due to productivity changes.

concepts.name: Perfect Competition
concepts.description: A market structure with many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry/exit, and firms that are price takers.

concepts.name: Monopoly
concepts.description: A market structure where a single firm supplies a product with no close substitutes and faces significant barriers to entry, allowing it to set price.

concepts.name: Monopolistic Competition
concepts.description: A market with many sellers offering differentiated products, some market power, and relatively free entry and exit.

concepts.name: Oligopoly
concepts.description: A market dominated by a few large firms; strategic interactions among them can lead to competition, collusion, or other game‑theoretic outcomes.

concepts.name: Gross Domestic Product
concepts.description: The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a specific period, measured via expenditure, income, or production approaches.

concepts.name: Circular Flow Model
concepts.description: A visual representation of the interactions between households (providing factors of production and consuming goods) and firms (producing goods and providing factor income).

concepts.name: Money
concepts.description: An asset widely accepted for transactions, serving as a medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value.

concepts.name: Banking System
concepts.description: Financial intermediaries that accept deposits, provide loans and other services, create deposits through lending, and manage credit, liquidity, and regulatory risks.

concepts.name: Monetary Policy
concepts.description: Actions by a central bank to influence financial conditions and macroeconomic outcomes, including adjusting policy interest rates, open-market operations, and managing liquidity, borrowing costs, and expectations.

concepts.name: Inflation
concepts.description: A sustained increase in the general price level, measured by a price index, which reduces purchasing power. Can arise from demand-pull pressures, cost-push factors, or expectations.

concepts.name: Unemployment
concepts.description: People without work, available for work, and actively seeking employment. Classified into frictional, structural, and cyclical types; measured against the labour force.

concepts.name: Phillips Curve
concepts.description: Framework describing the short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, where stronger demand reduces unemployment but increases inflationary pressure; long-run relationship is not a permanent trade-off due to expectations adjustment.

concepts.name: Fiscal Policy
concepts.description: Government decisions about spending, taxation, and borrowing to influence economic activity, including discretionary measures and automatic stabilisers like progressive taxes and unemployment transfers.

concepts.name: Fiscal Multiplier
concepts.description: The change in aggregate output resulting from a change in autonomous spending; size depends on leakages (saving, taxation, imports), marginal propensity to consume, supply constraints, and expectations.

concepts.name: Public Debt
concepts.description: Accumulated stock of government borrowing not yet repaid; sustainability depends on the relationship between interest rates, economic growth rate, primary fiscal balance, and existing debt stock.

concepts.name: Comparative Advantage
concepts.description: A country has comparative advantage in a product when it can produce it at a lower opportunity cost than another country; specialisation based on comparative advantage allows mutually beneficial trade.

concepts.name: Balance of Payments
concepts.description: Records of a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world, including current-account transactions (trade, income flows) and financial/capital transactions; a current-account deficit means spending exceeds receipts.

concepts.name: Exchange Rate
concepts.description: The price of one currency expressed in terms of another; influences import/export competitiveness, determined by supply and demand, interest-rate differences, inflation expectations, and capital movements.

concepts.name: Economic Development
concepts.description: Broader than economic growth; includes improvements in living standards, health, education, institutions, and participation. Measured by multiple indicators; human capital, infrastructure, and institutions are central.

concepts.name: Income Inequality
concepts.description: Differences in income across individuals or households, measured by shares and summary measures like the Gini coefficient; distinct from poverty; caused by skills, discrimination, inherited wealth, market power, or institutions.

concepts.name: Sustainable Economic Growth
concepts.description: Growth that increases wellbeing without undermining environmental and resource conditions for future generations; requires balancing current objectives with long-term environmental resilience.

concepts.name: Externalities
concepts.description: Costs or benefits that fall on people not directly involved in a transaction; examples include pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions from economic activity; addressed by taxes, tradable permits, regulation, and public investment.

concepts.name: Equilibrium
concepts.description: A market condition in which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

concepts.name: Elasticity
concepts.description: A measure of the responsiveness of one variable to a percentage change in another variable.
